notes: The take's premise is wrong: Premise 1 fails. It says the top 'Pro' tier is there mainly to make the middle plan look sensible, 'not so that people will buy it'. That misdescribes how tiered pricing works. In the research, a true decoy is an asymmetrically dominated option: it is worse than the target on everything, and almost nobody picks it (about 2% in Huber, Payne & Puto's studies). A Pro tier is not like that. It gives more for more money, and it is designed to be sold to buyers who are willing to pay more. This is called versioning, a form of second-degree price discrimination. The post's own iPhone example confirms the claim it relies on: Counterpoint estimates iPhone 18 Pro sales in India rose 28% year over year in the first three weeks. That shows the top tier is a real revenue line, not just a prop. Premise 2, that the page is built around the middle card where most of the money is made, is partly true. Firms do try to steer most buyers to the middle. But the post gives no evidence that the middle tier makes the most money, and the top tier usually earns the most per customer.. How it actually works: Firms use three tiers (Varian's 'Goldilocks pricing') to sort customers by how much they will pay. Price-sensitive buyers take Basic, most people take the middle, and buyers who want the most pay the high Pro price. The firm wants every tier to sell. On top of that, the compromise effect (Simonson, 1989) and extremeness aversion mean a middle option wins more share just by being in the middle, and a high price nearby acts as an anchor. So the top tier does make the middle look better, but that is a side benefit of a product the firm fully expects to sell, not the reason it exists. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

Could not verify: 'The 'Most Popular' ribbon on pricing cards is placed on the middle plan in advance, before any user clicks, rather than reflecting actual user choices.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.

mechanism.broken_premise: None fails. The 28% India figure checks out: Counterpoint estimated it for the first three weeks after launch. One nuance is that it covers the whole Pro series (18 Pro and Pro Max together), and Counterpoint says India's growth leaned toward the standard 18 Pro rather than the pricier Pro Max. It is also a third-party estimate, because Apple has not disclosed unit sales. This sharpens the claim rather than breaking it. The compromise effect is a real, named finding (Simonson 1989), and the post presents it as a tendency, not a rule.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: When an option sits in the middle of a set, it gains share. Its disadvantages look smaller against both ends, and it is the easiest choice to defend to others (Simonson 1989 calls this extremeness aversion and reason-based choice; Simonson & Tversky 1992 expand on it). Tiered pricing does two things at once: it sorts buyers by how much they are willing to pay, and it uses the premium tier as a real, profitable product that also makes the next tier down look reasonable. The Pro data fits this. Pro-series sales grew while buyers in India picked the 18 Pro over the costlier Pro Max, which is the compromise effect at work inside Apple's own lineup.

11f218deec69e576ed09dbb9e91c722f4ac1a119.broken_premise: Premise 1 fails. It says the top 'Pro' tier is there mainly to make the middle plan look sensible, 'not so that people will buy it'. That misdescribes how tiered pricing works. In the research, a true decoy is an asymmetrically dominated option: it is worse than the target on everything, and almost nobody picks it (about 2% in Huber, Payne & Puto's studies). A Pro tier is not like that. It gives more for more money, and it is designed to be sold to buyers who are willing to pay more. This is called versioning, a form of second-degree price discrimination. The post's own iPhone example confirms the claim it relies on: Counterpoint estimates iPhone 18 Pro sales in India rose 28% year over year in the first three weeks. That shows the top tier is a real revenue line, not just a prop. Premise 2, that the page is built around the middle card where most of the money is made, is partly true. Firms do try to steer most buyers to the middle. But the post gives no evidence that the middle tier makes the most money, and the top tier usually earns the most per customer.
11f218deec69e576ed09dbb9e91c722f4ac1a119.actual_mechanism: Firms use three tiers (Varian's 'Goldilocks pricing') to sort customers by how much they will pay. Price-sensitive buyers take Basic, most people take the middle, and buyers who want the most pay the high Pro price. The firm wants every tier to sell. On top of that, the compromise effect (Simonson, 1989) and extremeness aversion mean a middle option wins more share just by being in the middle, and a high price nearby acts as an anchor. So the top tier does make the middle look better, but that is a side benefit of a product the firm fully expects to sell, not the reason it exists.

cover.headline: The Pro plan sells, and makes the [middle plan] look smart
cover.sub: You skipped the expensive one and felt clever about it.

paragraphs: The 'Pro' plan does sell. But its other job is making the middle one look like a smart buy.
slides.why_swipe: Wait, what's wrong with the middle plan?

paragraphs: Every pricing page is the same three cards. Basic looks thin, Pro looks expensive, and the middle one has a little 'Most Popular' ribbon.
You pick it in under a minute and feel good for not overspending.
slides.why_swipe: Is this just apps, or everywhere?

paragraphs: Every app and gadget now comes in three tiers. The OTT app has Mobile, Standard and Premium.
At the café, the small latte is ₹220 and the large is ₹340, so ₹280 for the medium feels fair.
At the AC showroom, the salesman shows you the costliest model first. Then he says 'value for money' and walks you two steps left.
slides.why_swipe: Why does the top one even exist?

paragraphs: The top option is a real product. Some people want the most and will happily pay for it.
But it has a second job. It stands there looking expensive, so the price next to it feels sensible.
On its own, ₹280 for a coffee is a lot. Next to ₹340, it feels like self-control.
Three tiers sort you by how much you'll pay. The careful guy takes Basic, whoever wants everything takes Pro.
Most of us drift to the middle, because it's the easiest place to stand. It has a name: the compromise effect.
slides.why_swipe: But don't people buy the Pro too?

paragraphs: The Pro isn't a prop. iPhone 18 Pro sales in India jumped around 28% over last year in the first three weeks.
So the brand wins twice. The Pro crowd pays top price. Everyone else buys the middle and feels sensible.
slides.why_swipe: So are we just being fooled?

paragraphs: You're not dumb for this. You compared all three, so it feels like homework done.
Basic feels cheap, Pro feels like showing off. So you go middle, and nobody can say anything. That's the part you're really paying for.
slides.why_swipe: So whose idea was the middle plan?

paragraphs: "Medium hi le lete hain, sensible hai."
You say it like it was your idea. The pricing page was counting on it.

end.save: Come back to this the next time a pricing page shows you three cards.
end.send: Send to the friend who just upgraded to the 'smart middle plan' and told everyone about it.
end.promise: How brands really sell to us.

draft.alt_text: A ten-slide text post arguing that the expensive 'Pro' tier in three-tier pricing is a real product that sells, but also makes the middle option look sensible. It uses everyday examples such as pricing pages with a 'Most Popular' ribbon, OTT plans, café coffee sizes and AC showrooms. It explains that three tiers sort buyers by how much they will pay, and that most people drift to the middle, a pull called the compromise effect. It notes that iPhone 18 Pro sales in India rose around 28% over last year in the first three weeks, so the brand wins on both the top and the middle. It says picking the middle feels safe because nobody can call you cheap or a show-off, and ends with the line people say, 'Medium hi le lete hain, sensible hai,' noting the pricing page was counting on it.
